In this module, we will study why corrosion occurs, the electrochemical corrosion cell, factors that influence corrosion rate, common forms of corrosion, methods of corrosion prevention, cathodic protection, corrosion of different materials, concrete reinforcement corrosion, and the importance of good structural design for corrosion control. slide_002.text: Let us begin with the basic idea of corrosion. Corrosion is a natural process. Iron is produced from iron ore by using a large amount of energy, so the refined metal is in a relatively active or high-energy condition. When iron is exposed to the environment, it naturally tends to return toward a more stable form such as iron oxide, which we commonly call rust. This continuous tendency of iron to return to its stable state is described here as the corrosion cycle. Understanding this natural tendency is important because corrosion protection is essentially an effort to slow or interrupt that cycle. On this slide, we will develop the topic step by step. slide_003.text: Corrosion can be described as the deterioration or degradation of a metal or metal alloy by chemical or electrochemical means. For electrochemical corrosion to occur, four basic elements are required: an anode, a cathode, an electrical connection, and an electrolyte. These four elements together form a corrosion cell. If one or more of these essential elements is removed, the corrosion process can be interrupted. For example, removing or controlling the electrolyte can stop the electrochemical circuit from operating. This concept is fundamental because many corrosion prevention methods work by eliminating or controlling one part of the corrosion cell. On this slide, we will develop the topic step by step. slide_004.text: A corrosion cell consists of an anode, a cathode, a metallic pathway, and an electrolyte. The anode and cathode may be two different metals in direct contact, or they may simply be two different areas on the same piece of metal. Differences in impurities, crystalline structure, or electrochemical potential can create anodic and cathodic areas. The metallic pathway allows electron flow between these areas. The electrolyte can be seawater, rainwater, or even moisture present in the atmosphere. When all of these conditions exist together, the electrochemical reactions necessary for corrosion can proceed. slide_006.text: Now let us look at the reactions at the anode and cathode. At the anodic site, oxidation takes place. Metal atoms release electrons and enter the electrolyte as metal ions, so the metal thickness is reduced. This is where actual metal loss occurs. The released electrons move through the metallic path toward the cathode. At the cathodic site, a reduction reaction takes place. Oxygen and water participate in the reaction and consume the incoming electrons. A simple way to remember this is: the anode is associated with oxidation and metal loss, while the cathode is associated with reduction. On this slide, we will develop the topic step by step. slide_007.text: Several factors can increase or influence the corrosion rate. First is the electro-potential difference: the greater the difference between anodic and cathodic areas, the greater the corrosion tendency. Second is the relative size of the anode and cathode. A small anode connected to a large cathode can produce a high corrosion rate, while a large anode with a small cathode generally corrodes more slowly. Third is electrolyte conductivity, which depends strongly on ion concentration. Seawater therefore causes faster corrosion than fresh water because it contains more dissolved salts. Temperature is another factor; higher temperature generally increases corrosion rate, while lower temperature reduces it. On this slide, we will develop the topic step by step. slide_008.text: Other important factors include pH, humidity, pollution, and passivity. Metals react differently depending on the pH of their environment. According to this material, steel corrodes more readily in acidic conditions, while strong alkaline conditions can reduce corrosion. High relative humidity promotes corrosion because it provides moisture for the electrolyte. Pollution, acid rain, and chemicals can also accelerate corrosion. Passivity works in the opposite direction. Some metals form a stable oxide film on their surface, and this passive layer can reduce the rate of further corrosion as long as it remains intact. The key principle is that corrosion control is often most effective when several protective methods are combined rather than relying on a single measure. slide_010.text: Environmental control is another way to reduce corrosion, but its use depends on the location. In an open outside atmosphere, the environment generally cannot be controlled. In enclosed, confined, or encapsulated spaces, however, conditions can be managed. A dehumidifier can reduce moisture in the air, ventilation can remove trapped humid air and improve circulation, and heating can raise the temperature and help prevent condensation. These methods reduce the availability of moisture, which is an important part of the electrolyte. Environmental control is therefore especially useful in enclosed areas where humidity and condensation can be managed. On this slide, we will develop the topic step by step. slide_011.text: When evaluating corrosion risk, an inspector should look at both the material and the structural details. Sharp edges, corners, rough weld seams, blowholes, and weld spatter can create vulnerable areas. Bi-metallic combinations may create galvanic corrosion. Poor drainage, stagnant water, and water accumulation can provide a persistent electrolyte. Limited access can make painting and maintenance difficult, especially around notches, stitch welds, crevices, and narrow gaps. Flow conditions such as turbulence and cavitation also matter. Exposure to aggressive ions, chemicals, outdoor conditions, temperature, humidity, and different forms of stress should all be considered during corrosion assessment. slide_012.text: Corrosion can have serious economic and safety consequences. Economically, corrosion may require the replacement of damaged equipment, additional material through overdesign, preventive maintenance such as painting, and even shutdown of equipment after corrosion failure. The safety consequences can be more serious. A corroded structure can lose strength and become unsafe, creating risks to people, property, and the environment. This is why corrosion protection should not be viewed only as a maintenance expense. It is an essential part of preserving structural reliability, reducing unplanned costs, and maintaining safe operation throughout the service life of equipment and structures. Metallic coatings create a dense barrier layer, while paints and coatings can protect through barrier, inhibitive, or cathodic effects. Corrosion inhibitors form a passive protective layer. slide_014.text: Corrosion inhibitors are chemical compounds that are introduced into a corrosive environment in small quantities to reduce, slow, or prevent corrosion. They can react with water and steel and help form a passive protective layer. Inhibitors may be added continuously or intermittently to systems such as acids, cooling water, steam, and other process environments. Examples listed in the material include phosphate, chromate, nitrite, silicate, molybdate, and organic inhibitors, as well as oxygen scavengers. They may be used in coatings as inhibitive pigments or in liquid systems. Their purpose is to reduce rusting and anodic corrosion by changing the corrosive environment or forming a protective film. slide_016.text: The galvanic series is a list or arrangement of metals and alloys according to their electrochemical potential in a particular environment, commonly seawater. It is also referred to here as the nobility series. Active metals such as magnesium, zinc, and aluminium are more anodic and tend to corrode more easily. More noble materials such as gold, titanium, and graphite are more cathodic and tend to corrode less readily. The galvanic series is useful when different metals are connected together because the relative position of the metals helps indicate which material is more likely to become the anode and corrode. slide_023.text: Pitting corrosion is a localized form of corrosion that often develops on metals protected by a passive film. When that protective film is damaged by abrasion, salts, or chemical attack, small local pits can form. The top of the pit has greater oxygen availability and acts as the cathodic region, while the bottom of the pit has less oxygen and becomes anodic. As the pit becomes deeper, oxygen availability at the bottom decreases further and localized attack can accelerate. Pitting is dangerous because early stages can be difficult to detect, while penetration can become deep and irregular. Its shape can also make repair more difficult than uniform surface corrosion. slide_039.text: This slide covers the first two stages of concrete repair. The first step is to remove loose and damaged concrete around the affected area so that sound material is exposed and the deteriorated repair zone is accessible. Only unsound concrete should be removed while preserving sound surrounding material. The second step is to identify and remove carbonated concrete. A pH indicator paper or indicator solution can be used to locate concrete where alkalinity has been reduced. Carbonated material should be removed.

slide_040.text: The next stages are to shape the repair area and prepare the reinforcement. The repair boundary should be formed into a sound, neat profile, with loose edges cut back so the repair material can bond properly. If the reinforcing steel has suffered significant section loss, it may need to be renewed or replaced using an appropriate lap or coupler. After that, the exposed reinforcement should be blast cleaned or mechanically cleaned. Rust, mill scale, and loose corrosion products must be removed.

slide_041.text: This slide completes the remaining stages of the repair procedure. First, corrosion protection is applied to the cleaned reinforcement, using an alkali-resistant anti-corrosive coating such as an epoxy primer. Full coverage of the exposed steel is important. Next, compatible repair mortar or new concrete is placed into the prepared area, compacted, and finished so that the original section and surface profile are restored. Finally, a carbonation-inhibitive protective coating is applied over the repaired surface and surrounding concrete. This top coat helps.

Blast cleaning can also reveal fabrication defects such as raised slivers or laminations. slide_060.text: Structures should be designed so that water and contaminants cannot collect. Rainwater, splashed seawater, and airborne pollutants can combine to form an effective electrolyte and accelerate corrosion. Good drainage reduces the time that steel remains wet. The shape of structural members should encourage water to run off easily, and drain openings should be located where trapped liquid can escape. Pockets, recesses, and other water traps should be avoided. These simple design decisions can significantly reduce corrosion because they reduce the duration and concentration of moisture and contaminants on the steel surface. Open sections should have drain holes so trapped water can escape, and their internal surfaces must be protected where required. Closed sections should be completely airtight and watertight, with continuous welds sealing the edges and covers or caps closing openings. The slide explains that a fully welded and sealed closed box can avoid internal corrosion because electrolyte cannot enter. However, temporary seals, removable covers, or bolted joints may allow moisture ingress. If moisture can enter but cannot drain or dry, corrosion may become difficult to control. slide_063.text: These design examples show why geometry and accessibility are important for corrosion protection. The diagrams compare structural sections and spacing requirements so that surfaces can be reached for surface preparation, coating application, inspection, and maintenance. The connection detail also shows features such as a weld access hole, backing bar, beam flange, and shear tab, all of which can create difficult-to-coat locations if not properly designed. The drainage examples compare poor details that trap water with better arrangements that allow water to escape and best arrangements that are naturally self-draining. The key design principle is to avoid inaccessible gaps and water traps wherever possible.

slide_064.text: This slide illustrates the use of insulating gaskets and washers in connections between dissimilar metals. When two different metals are in electrical contact and moisture is present, a galvanic cell can form. Insulating materials interrupt the metallic electrical connection between the components and therefore help reduce galvanic corrosion. The examples show insulation placed between joint faces and around bolts or fasteners so that the dissimilar metals are separated electrically. This design approach is particularly useful where dissimilar metals must be used together and complete material substitution is not practical. Good isolation, sealing, and maintenance of the insulating components are important for continued protection.
